title: Derandomized Online-to-Non-convex Conversion for Stochastic Weakly Convex Optimization
claim: Our proposed optimizer reaches lower training loss and higher accuracy faster than the standard momentum baseline across architectures.
layout: 2x3 grid of line plots; rows by architecture, columns by metric
description: A 2-row by 3-column grid of training-curve line plots comparing three methods: SGDM in red/pink and D-O2NC with T=20 (green) and T=50 (blue). The top row is ResNet-101 on CIFAR-10 over 400 epochs. The bottom row is ViT over 600 epochs. Columns show train loss, train accuracy and test accuracy. Shaded bands show variance. The green and blue curves drop in loss and rise in accuracy faster than the red curve, especially on ResNet-101 in the early epochs. The gap narrows by the end of training. Legends sit in each panel. Each panel has a serif caption below it, such as '(a) Train Loss (ResNet-101)'. The eye goes first to the steep early curves in the top-left panel.
caption: Experimental results on CIFAR-10 with ResNet-101 (top) and ViT (bottom) networks.
abstract: Online-to-non-convex conversion (O2NC) is an online updates learning framework for producing Goldstein $(\delta,\epsilon)$-stationary points of non-smooth non-convex functions with optimal oracle complexity $\mathcal{O}(\delta^{-1} \epsilon^{-3})$. Subject to auxiliary \emph{random interpolation or scaling}, O2NC recapitulates the stochastic gradient descent with momentum (SGDM) algorithm popularly used for training neural networks. Randomization, however, introduces deviations from practical SGDM. So a natural question arises: Can we derandomize O2NC to achieve the same optimal guarantees while resembling SGDM? On the negative side, the general answer is \emph{no} due to the impossibility results of~\citet{jordan23deterministic}, showing that no dimension-free rate can be achieved by deterministic algorithms. On the positive side, as the primary contribution of the present work, we show that O2NC can be naturally derandomized for \emph{weakly convex} functions. Remarkably, our deterministic algorithm converges at an optimal rate as long as the weak convexity parameter is no larger than $\mathcal{O}(\delta^{-1}\epsilon^{-1})$. In other words, the stronger stationarity is expected, the higher non-convexity can be tolerated by our optimizer. Additionally, we develop a periodically restarted variant of our method to enable more progressive updates when the iterates are far from stationarity. The resulting algorithm, which can be viewed as a momentum-restarted variant of SGDM, has been empirically demonstrated to be effective and efficient for training ResNet and ViT models.
